entries.meaning: To teach someone over a long period, especially in a school or college. ---
examples: Public schools educate nearly fifty million American children.
She was educated at a small college in Vermont.
The campaign is educating parents about online safety.

entries.meaning: To teach one student or a very small group, usually privately. ---
examples: He tutors high school students in chemistry.
She tutored me all through my senior year.
I have been tutoring since my first semester.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (tutor a student in math), intransitive (she tutors on weekends)

entries.meaning: To advise and guide a less experienced person over a long time. ---
examples: Senior nurses mentor everyone who joins the unit.
She mentored three graduate students last year.
He has mentored dozens of young teachers.

entries.meaning: To train a person or team, or prepare someone for a test or performance. ---
examples: She coaches students for the SAT every spring.
He coached debate for ten years.
They are coaching her through the interview.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (coach a debate team), intransitive (he coaches at the middle school)
entries.contrast: The third-person form adds -es: coaches.

entries.meaning: To teach your own children at home instead of sending them to school. ---
examples: They homeschool their three children.
She was homeschooled until ninth grade.
More families are homeschooling this year.
entries.русский: обучать на дому, давать домашнее образование
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (they homeschool their kids), intransitive (the family homeschools)
entries.contrast: Written as one word in American English: homeschool, homeschooled.

entries.meaning: To learn, or to teach someone, a new set of skills for different work. ---
examples: The company will retrain anyone whose job disappears.
She retrained as a math teacher at forty.
He is retraining for a job in health care.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (retrain the staff), intransitive (he retrained as a nurse)

entries.meaning: To give someone the information they need before they do something. ---
examples: The coach briefs the team before every game.
We were briefed on the new grading policy.
She is briefing the substitute teacher now.
entries.contrast: You brief someone on something.

entries.meaning: To talk through what happened after a task, a lesson, or a test. ---
examples: The instructor debriefs the class after every simulation.
They debriefed us as soon as the exercise ended.
We spent an hour debriefing after the presentation.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (debrief the students), intransitive (we debrief every Friday)

entries.meaning: To gradually put an attitude or a habit into someone's mind. ---
examples: Good teachers instill curiosity, not just facts.
Her father instilled a love of reading in her.
The program is instilling better study habits.
entries.contrast: American instill, British instil; the l doubles before endings: instilled, instilling.

entries.meaning: To pass knowledge or information on to other people. ---
examples: A lecture can impart facts but not judgment.
She imparted everything she knew about the trade.
He has imparted his method to a whole generation of teachers.

entries.meaning: To explain something to someone so that they finally understand it. ---
examples: Maybe you can enlighten me about the new rules.
The lecture enlightened nobody.
She has enlightened us on how the system really works.

entries.meaning: To make someone familiar with something new. ---
examples: The first week acquaints students with the library.
We acquainted ourselves with the rules before the exam.
He is acquainting the class with the lab equipment.
entries.contrast: You acquaint someone with something.

entries.meaning: To learn about something, or teach someone about it, until it feels familiar. ---
examples: Take an hour to familiarize yourself with the software.
She familiarized the new students with the campus.
We are familiarizing ourselves with the syllabus.
entries.contrast: American familiarize, British familiarise. You familiarize someone with something.

entries.meaning: To help someone get used to a new place or situation. ---
examples: A short video orients new students.
They oriented us on the first day of class.
I am still orienting myself in this building.
entries.contrast: Americans write orient; the British often write orientate.

entries.meaning: To be a clear example of something, or to show it by example. ---
examples: These two sentences exemplify the rule.
Her essay exemplified everything we had practiced.
He has exemplified the standard we expect from seniors.
entries.contrast: Consonant + -y changes: exemplifies, exemplified, but exemplifying keeps the y.

entries.meaning: To say something again so that it is understood. ---
examples: Let me reiterate the main point.
She reiterated the deadline twice.
He kept reiterating that the exam would be open book.

entries.meaning: To give a test, or to carry out an official procedure. ---
examples: The state administers the reading test every spring.
A nurse administered the hearing screening.
They are administering the exam in the gym.

entries.meaning: To watch over students while they take an exam. ---
examples: Two graduate students proctor the final.
She proctored the makeup exam last Saturday.
I am proctoring in room 12 tomorrow.
entries.русский: следить за порядком на экзамене, быть наблюдателем
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (proctor the final), intransitive (she proctors on Saturdays)
entries.contrast: American proctor; the British say invigilate.

entries.meaning: To see or show the difference between two things. ---
examples: Beginners cannot differentiate these two vowels.
She differentiated between fact and opinion.
The teacher is differentiating her lessons for three reading levels.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (differentiate the two sounds), intransitive (differentiate between them)
entries.contrast: You differentiate between A and B, or differentiate A from B.

entries.meaning: To add something extra to what is already there. ---
examples: Short videos supplement the textbook.
She supplemented the lecture with a handout.
He is supplementing his income by tutoring.
entries.contrast: The verb ends in a full -ment: SUP-luh-ment. The noun a supplement ends weakly: SUP-luh-muhnt.

entries.meaning: To make something easier, or to lead a discussion or workshop. ---
examples: Small classes facilitate real discussion.
She facilitated the writing workshop last summer.
The grant has facilitated a new tutoring program.

entries.meaning: To help someone, especially with part of a task. ---
examples: Volunteers assist students with their homework.
She assisted the professor for two semesters.
He is assisting in the chemistry lab this year.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (assist a student), intransitive (assist with the lab)
entries.contrast: You assist someone with something, or assist in doing it.

entries.meaning: To make it easier for someone to do something. ---
examples: Can you help me with these verbs?
She helped me study for the final.
He has helped dozens of students pass the exam.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (help your classmate), intransitive (she always helps)
entries.contrast: After help, the bare infinitive is normal: help me study (also possible: help me to study).

entries.meaning: To help something happen or work better. ---
examples: Pictures aid memory more than rereading does.
A quiet room aided her concentration.
Flashcards have aided thousands of language learners.

entries.meaning: To encourage a skill, a feeling, or a habit to develop. ---
examples: Group projects foster cooperation.
That teacher fostered my interest in science.
The program has fostered real progress in reading.

entries.meaning: To make someone more interested, active, or eager to think. ---
examples: Good questions stimulate thinking.
The film stimulated a long discussion.
The class is stimulating her interest in history.

entries.meaning: To hold someone's interest, or to get seriously involved with something. ---
examples: A good lesson engages every student in the room.
She engaged the class with a story about her grandmother.
They are engaging more deeply with the text this year.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (engage the class), intransitive (engage with the material)
entries.contrast: You engage with a text or a person; the -e drops before -ing: engaging.

entries.meaning: To make someone lose confidence, or to try to stop them doing something. ---
examples: Harsh grading can discourage beginners.
A bad first semester discouraged him completely.
The school is discouraging students from taking five AP classes.
entries.contrast: You discourage someone from doing something.

entries.meaning: To tell someone officially that they have done something wrong. ---
examples: Teachers rarely reprimand a student in front of the class.
She was reprimanded for copying an essay.
The dean is reprimanding both of them this afternoon.

entries.meaning: To make someone suffer a penalty for breaking a rule. ---
examples: Some teachers punish late work with a lower grade.
He was punished for cheating on the quiz.
They are punishing the whole class for one prank.
entries.contrast: The third-person form adds -es: punishes. You punish someone for something.

entries.meaning: To praise someone publicly or officially. ---
examples: The principal commends the students who improve the most.
She was commended for her research.
He has commended the class twice this month.
entries.contrast: Not the same as recommend, which suggests rather than praises.

entries.meaning: To forgive a small fault, or to officially let someone miss something. ---
examples: The office will excuse an absence with a note from home.
She excused him from gym class for a week.
You are excused from the final if your average is above 95.
entries.contrast: The verb ends in a z sound (ik-SKYOOZ); the noun an excuse ends in s (ik-SKYOOS).

entries.meaning: To officially join a school, a class, or a program. ---
examples: You can enroll in the course online.
She enrolled her son in a summer program.
Over four hundred students have enrolled this fall.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (enroll a child in school), intransitive (enroll in a course)
entries.contrast: American enroll, British enrol; the l doubles: enrolled, enrolling. You enroll in a class.

entries.meaning: To ask formally to be accepted somewhere, or to put a rule or method to use. ---
examples: She wants to apply to three universities.
He applied for a scholarship in December.
We are applying what we learned last week.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (apply the rule), intransitive (apply to a college)
entries.contrast: Consonant + -y changes: applies, applied, but applying keeps the y. You apply to a school for a place.

entries.meaning: To send in an application a second time. ---
examples: If they turn you down, you can reapply next year.
She reapplied in the fall and got in.
He is reapplying to the same program.
entries.contrast: Consonant + -y changes: reapplies, reapplied, but reapplying keeps the y.

entries.meaning: To put someone on a list of people waiting for a place. ---
examples: Popular seminars waitlist twenty or thirty students.
She was waitlisted at her first-choice college.
The registrar is waitlisting everyone who applied late.
entries.contrast: Usually heard in the passive: be waitlisted.

entries.meaning: To put something off until a later date. ---
examples: You may defer admission for one year.
He deferred his enrollment and worked abroad.
She is deferring the exam because of illness.
entries.contrast: The stress is on the last syllable, so the r doubles: deferred, deferring.

entries.meaning: To finish a course of study and receive a diploma or a degree. ---
examples: She will graduate in May.
He graduated from Ohio State in 2019.
Two hundred seniors are graduating this spring.
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive (she graduates in May), transitive (the school graduates 300 seniors a year)
entries.contrast: Americans graduate from a school. The verb is GRAJ-oo-ayt; the noun a graduate is GRAJ-oo-uht.

entries.meaning: To reach the standard needed for a job, a place, or the next round. ---
examples: These two courses qualify you for the certificate.
She qualified as a nurse last year.
He is qualifying for the state finals.
entries.русский: получать квалификацию; давать право; проходить отбор
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (the course qualifies you to teach), intransitive (she qualified as a nurse)
entries.contrast: Consonant + -y changes: qualifies, qualified, but qualifying keeps the y. You qualify for something or as something.

entries.meaning: To study one subject as your main field at an American college. ---
examples: I want to major in linguistics.
She majored in biology.
He is majoring in computer science.
entries.contrast: An American student majors in a subject; a British student simply studies it.

entries.meaning: To concentrate on one narrow area of study or work. ---
examples: Doctors specialize after medical school.
She specialized in medieval history.
The school is specializing in the arts.
entries.contrast: American specialize, British specialise. You specialize in something.

entries.meaning: To officially recognize a school or program as meeting a standard. ---
examples: A regional board accredits the nursing program.
The state accredited the school in 2018.
They are accrediting the online degree this year.
entries.contrast: Two c's but only one t: accredited, accrediting.

entries.meaning: To work somewhere for a short time, often unpaid, in order to learn the job. ---
examples: Many students intern the summer before senior year.
She interned at a law firm in Chicago.
He is interning with a local newspaper.
entries.contrast: The verb is stressed at the end (in-TURN); the noun an intern at the front (IN-turn).

entries.meaning: To follow someone at work for a day or two in order to learn what the job is like. ---
examples: Juniors can shadow a nurse for a day.
He shadowed an engineer last spring.
She is shadowing a veterinarian this week.
entries.русский: сопровождать (специалиста) для обучения, наблюдать за работой

entries.meaning: To learn a trade by working under a skilled person. ---
examples: Young carpenters still apprentice under a master.
He apprenticed with a violin maker for four years.
She is apprenticing at a bakery this year.
entries.contrast: The third-person form adds -s to the silent e: apprentices.

entries.meaning: To go along with a group of young people in order to look after them. ---
examples: Parents chaperone every field trip.
My dad chaperoned the eighth-grade dance.
She is chaperoning the trip to Washington.
entries.contrast: Also written chaperon, but chaperone is usual in American English.

entries.meaning: To study very hard in a short time just before a test. ---
examples: Try not to cram the night before the exam.
We crammed for six hours straight.
He is cramming for the chemistry final.
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive (cram for a test), transitive (cram three chapters into one night)
entries.contrast: The m doubles: crammed, cramming. You cram for a test.

entries.meaning: To get ready, or get someone ready, for something. ---
examples: I need to prep for tomorrow's quiz.
She prepped her students for the interview.
He is prepping for the bar exam.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (prep the students), intransitive (prep for the test)
entries.contrast: The p doubles: prepped, prepping. Informal short form of prepare.

entries.meaning: To keep something in your memory. ---
examples: Most people retain very little from a long lecture.
She retained almost everything she read.
He is retaining far more since he started using flashcards.

entries.meaning: To learn something so thoroughly that it becomes automatic. ---
examples: Children internalize grammar rules without being taught them.
She had internalized her teacher's high standards.
You are internalizing the pattern every time you repeat it.
entries.contrast: American internalize, British internalise.

entries.meaning: To come back to a topic in order to look at it again. ---
examples: We will revisit this topic in chapter nine.
The class revisited the poem before the test.
I am revisiting my notes from last semester.

entries.meaning: To improve a skill by practicing it carefully over time. ---
examples: Reading aloud every day hones your pronunciation.
She honed her writing in a summer workshop.
He has honed the technique over twenty years.
entries.contrast: Drop the -e before -ing: honing.

entries.meaning: To make what you have learned firmer, or to combine several things into one. ---
examples: A short review consolidates everything from the week.
Sleep consolidated the day's practice.
They are consolidating two classes into one.

entries.meaning: To combine ideas from several sources into one whole. ---
examples: The essay asks you to synthesize three readings.
She synthesized the articles into a single argument.
They are synthesizing data from four studies.
entries.contrast: American synthesize, British synthesise.

entries.meaning: To draw a broad conclusion from only a few cases. ---
examples: Learners often generalize a rule and use it where it does not fit.
He generalized from a single example.
She is generalizing about a whole country.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (generalize the rule), intransitive (try not to generalize)
entries.contrast: You generalize from evidence or about a group. American -ize, British -ise.

entries.meaning: To connect one thing with another in your mind. ---
examples: Try to associate each new word with a picture.
She associated the smell of chalk with school.
I have always associated that book with my first teacher.
entries.contrast: You associate one thing with another. The verb ends -ayt; the noun an associate ends -uht.

entries.meaning: To connect two things, or to understand and feel close to something. ---
examples: Good teaching relates new facts to what students already know.
She related the story to her own childhood.
I could not relate to that character at all.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (relate the two ideas), intransitive (relate to a character)
entries.contrast: relate to something means to understand it or feel connected to it.

entries.meaning: To say that something was caused by or made by a particular person or thing. ---
examples: Students often attribute that quote to Mark Twain.
She attributed her success to one teacher.
He is attributing every bad grade to bad luck.
entries.contrast: The verb is uh-TRIB-yoot; the noun an attribute is AT-ruh-byoot. You attribute something to someone.

entries.meaning: To work something out from a starting point, or to come originally from a source. ---
examples: You can derive the whole formula from two simple rules.
The word derived from Latin.
We are deriving the equation step by step.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (derive the formula), intransitive (the word derives from Latin)
entries.contrast: Something derives from a source; drop the -e before -ing: deriving.

entries.meaning: To break a sentence into its grammatical parts, or to work out what a hard text means. ---
examples: First-year students parse Latin sentences every day.
I could not parse that question at all.
She is still parsing the instructions.

entries.meaning: To look carefully for something. ---
examples: Search the index for the term.
I searched for an hour and found nothing.
She is searching the database for older studies.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (search the index), intransitive (search for a source)
entries.contrast: You search for a thing, but you search a place: search the library means look through it.

entries.meaning: To check something a second time to be sure it is right. ---
examples: Double-check your answers before you hand in the test.
She double-checked every calculation.
I am double-checking the spelling of his name.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (double-check your answers), intransitive (double-check before you submit)
entries.contrast: Written with a hyphen: double-check, double-checked, double-checking.

entries.meaning: To look at something again in order to judge it properly. ---
examples: Historians reexamine old evidence all the time.
She reexamined her notes after class.
We are reexamining the first three chapters.
entries.contrast: American writing usually joins it up: reexamine (British re-examine).

entries.meaning: To judge or measure something again, usually after new information. ---
examples: Teachers reassess every student at the end of the unit.
The school reassessed his reading level in March.
They are reassessing the whole curriculum.
entries.contrast: The third-person form adds -es: reassesses.

entries.meaning: To do a piece of work again in a different or better way. ---
examples: You may rework the essay for a higher grade.
She reworked the problem three times before it came out right.
He is reworking his introduction.

entries.meaning: To repeat an experiment or a result exactly. ---
examples: Students replicate a famous experiment in week three.
No one could replicate her results.
They are replicating the study with older children.

entries.meaning: To try something new in order to see what happens. ---
examples: We experiment with different study methods every term.
She experimented with flashcards for a month.
He is experimenting with teaching the whole class in Spanish.
entries.contrast: You experiment with a method and experiment on a subject.

entries.meaning: To suggest an explanation that can then be tested. ---
examples: Scientists hypothesize first and test afterward.
She hypothesized that sleep improves recall.
We are hypothesizing about the cause.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (hypothesize that sleep helps), intransitive (scientists hypothesize, then test)
entries.contrast: American hypothesize, British hypothesise.

entries.meaning: To form an idea about why something is as it is, without full proof. ---
examples: Historians still theorize about why the city fell.
He theorized that the text had two authors.
They are theorizing with very little evidence.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (theorize that the text had two authors), intransitive (theorize about the cause)

entries.meaning: To prove that a statement or an argument is wrong. ---
examples: Your job in the debate is to refute the other side.
She refuted the claim in two sentences.
He has refuted every point so far.

entries.meaning: To confuse someone completely. ---
examples: English spelling perplexes almost every learner.
The last question perplexed even the teacher.
The results have perplexed researchers for years.
entries.contrast: The third-person form adds -es: perplexes.

entries.meaning: To ask something so hard that the other person cannot answer. ---
examples: That riddle stumps everyone.
The last problem stumped me completely.
She has stumped the whole class with one question.

entries.meaning: To take someone's attention away from what they are doing. ---
examples: Phones distract everyone in the room.
The noise distracted me during the whole exam.
She is distracting the entire back row.
entries.contrast: You distract someone from their work.

entries.meaning: To pay attention to a sound, a person, or a recording. ---
examples: Listen to the recording twice before you answer.
She listened to the lecture again at double speed.
I have been listening to podcasts to train my ear.
entries.contrast: The t is silent. You listen to something — never listen the radio.

entries.meaning: To put an idea into clear words, or to pronounce sounds clearly. ---
examples: Try to articulate exactly what you do not understand.
She articulated the problem better than the professor did.
He is learning to articulate his ideas in English.
entries.contrast: The verb ends ar-TIK-yuh-layt; the adjective articulate ends ar-TIK-yuh-luht.

entries.meaning: To pronounce words clearly and distinctly. ---
examples: Enunciate every syllable when you read aloud.
She enunciated each word for the beginners.
He is enunciating much better after a month of practice.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (enunciate each syllable), intransitive (enunciate clearly)

entries.meaning: To say a word with the wrong sounds or the wrong stress. ---
examples: Almost everyone mispronounces my last name.
He mispronounced the word colonel in front of the whole class.
She is afraid of mispronouncing words out loud.
entries.contrast: The third-person form adds -es: mispronounces.

entries.meaning: To have a real conversation, especially in a foreign language. ---
examples: By May the class can converse in simple Spanish.
We conversed in French for an hour.
She is conversing with a native speaker twice a week.
entries.contrast: The verb is kuhn-VURS; the noun the converse (the opposite) is KAHN-vurs. You converse with someone.

entries.meaning: To match something else, or to exchange letters with someone. ---
examples: The numbers in the margin correspond to the notes at the back.
They corresponded for two years before they met.
She has been corresponding with a class in Japan.
entries.contrast: A thing corresponds to another thing; a person corresponds with another person.

entries.meaning: To pass a message or information on to someone else. ---
examples: Please relay the assignment to anyone who was absent.
She relayed the principal's message to the class.
He is relaying the questions to the speaker.
entries.contrast: A vowel before -y keeps the y: relays, relayed, never relaid.

entries.meaning: To describe something fully, point by point. ---
examples: The syllabus details every assignment.
She detailed her method in the appendix.
The handbook is detailing the new rules for next fall.
entries.contrast: The verb is stressed at the end: di-TAYL. The noun a detail is usually DEE-tayl.

entries.meaning: To watch a recording or a video again. ---
examples: You can rewatch the lecture as many times as you like.
She rewatched the lab demonstration twice.
He is rewatching last week's class before the quiz.
entries.contrast: The third-person form adds -es: rewatches.

entries.meaning: To gain an advantage from something, or to do someone good. ---
examples: Slower readers benefit from extra practice.
She benefited from a year abroad.
The whole class is benefiting from the smaller size.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (the change benefits everyone), intransitive (benefit from extra practice)
entries.contrast: American English keeps one t: benefited, benefiting (British often benefitted). You benefit from something.

entries.meaning: To do what a rule, a promise, or a requirement asks for. ---
examples: Two lab courses fulfill the science requirement.
She fulfilled the language requirement with Spanish.
He is fulfilling his last credits this summer.
entries.contrast: American fulfill, British fulfil; both double the l before endings: fulfilled, fulfilling.

entries.meaning: To do what a rule or an order requires. ---
examples: All students must comply with the honor code.
The school complied with the new state rules.
They are complying fully with the policy.
entries.contrast: You comply with a rule. Consonant + -y changes: complies, complied.

entries.meaning: To act in a particular way, or to act properly. ---
examples: The kids behave better with a substitute than with me.
He behaved beautifully all semester.
They are behaving as if the test did not matter.
entries.contrast: On its own, behave means behave well; with a reflexive it is stronger: behave yourself.

entries.meaning: To act badly, especially in class. ---
examples: Two boys always misbehave in the back row.
She misbehaved only once all year.
He was sent to the office for misbehaving.

entries.meaning: To break the rules of a test or a game in order to gain an advantage. ---
examples: Nobody needs to cheat on a take-home exam.
He cheated on the final and was expelled.
She was caught cheating in the first week.
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive (cheat on a test), transitive (cheat someone out of money)
entries.contrast: You cheat on a test and cheat at cards.

entries.meaning: To keep going despite difficulty, or to continue to exist. ---
examples: Students who persist through the first year usually finish.
She persisted until the proof finally worked.
The problem is persisting into the second semester.
entries.contrast: You persist in doing something, or persist with a task.

entries.meaning: To keep trying at something hard for a long time. ---
examples: You have to persevere through the difficult chapters.
She persevered and finished the degree in five years.
He is persevering after two failed attempts.
entries.contrast: Note the three e's: per-se-vere. You persevere with a task or in doing something.

entries.meaning: To try to do something, especially something difficult. ---
examples: Attempt every question, even if you are unsure.
She attempted the bonus problem and got it right.
He is attempting the exam for the third time.
entries.contrast: You attempt to do something, never attempt do something.

entries.meaning: To start dealing with a difficult problem or task. ---
examples: Tackle the hardest question first.
She tackled the whole reading list over the summer.
We are tackling fractions this week.

entries.meaning: To manage successfully with something difficult. ---
examples: Some freshmen cannot cope with the workload.
She coped well with a heavy schedule.
He is coping better since the tutoring started.
entries.contrast: You cope with something; drop the -e before -ing: coping.

entries.meaning: To achieve what you were trying to do. ---
examples: Students succeed when someone expects them to.
She succeeded on her second try.
He has succeeded in every class he has taken.
entries.contrast: You succeed in doing something, or succeed at a subject.

entries.meaning: To be extremely good at something. ---
examples: She excels at languages.
He excelled in math but struggled with writing.
They are excelling in the new program.
entries.contrast: The l doubles: excelled, excelling. You excel at or in something.

entries.meaning: To do better than someone or something else. ---
examples: Small classes usually outperform large ones.
She outperformed every student in her year.
The new method is outperforming the old one.

entries.meaning: To go beyond someone or something in quality or amount. ---
examples: Her essay surpasses anything else in the class.
He surpassed his own record on the third try.
The results have surpassed what anyone expected.
entries.contrast: The third-person form adds -es: surpasses.

entries.meaning: To try to win or to do better than others. ---
examples: Ten schools compete in the spelling bee.
She competed in the science fair twice.
They are competing for two scholarships.
entries.contrast: You compete with or against someone for something.
entries.phrasal verbs: compete with, compete against, compete for

entries.meaning: To fail a test or a course, or to give someone a failing grade. ---
examples: If you skip the final, you flunk the course.
He flunked chemistry and had to take it again.
She is flunking two classes this semester.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (flunk chemistry), intransitive (half the class flunked)
entries.contrast: Informal American English for fail.

entries.meaning: To do extremely well on a test or in an interview. ---
examples: If you study tonight, you will ace this quiz.
She aced the interview.
He has aced every test so far this year.
entries.contrast: Drop the -e before -ing: acing. Informal American English.

entries.meaning: To take an active part in something. ---
examples: Part of your grade is how often you participate.
She participated in every discussion.
Only half the class is participating today.
entries.contrast: You participate in something.

entries.meaning: To work together with someone toward the same goal. ---
examples: The two schools cooperate on a summer program.
He cooperated fully with the investigation.
They are cooperating on a joint project.
entries.contrast: Americans write cooperate without a hyphen (British often co-operate). You cooperate with someone on something.

entries.meaning: To join with another person or group in order to work together. ---
examples: Partner with someone you have not worked with yet.
She partnered with a classmate for the lab report.
Our school is partnering with a community college.
entries.contrast: You partner with someone.

entries.meaning: To spend time with other people in a friendly way. ---
examples: Freshmen mostly socialize in the dorms.
We socialized for an hour after the exam.
She is socializing much more this year.
entries.contrast: American socialize, British socialise.

entries.meaning: To become a friend to someone, especially someone new or alone. ---
examples: Older students befriend the newcomers in September.
She befriended a girl from Brazil.
He has befriended everyone on his floor.

entries.meaning: To be owned by someone, or to feel accepted in a place. ---
examples: This textbook belongs to the library.
She never felt she belonged at that school.
Children learn better when they feel they belong.
entries.contrast: belong to someone means it is theirs; with no preposition it means being in the right place.

entries.meaning: To get used to a new place, climate, or situation. ---
examples: It takes about a month to acclimate to college.
She acclimated quickly to the new school.
He is still acclimating to classes taught in English.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (acclimate the new students), intransitive (acclimate to college)
entries.contrast: Americans say acclimate; the British say acclimatize. You acclimate to something.

entries.meaning: To say numbers in order or find a total, or to matter toward a result. ---
examples: First graders count to a hundred by tens.
She counted the votes twice.
I am counting the days until graduation.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (count the pages), intransitive (this quiz counts)

entries.meaning: To take one number away from another. ---
examples: Subtract seven from twelve.
The teacher subtracted five points for turning it in late.
We are subtracting fractions this week.
entries.contrast: You subtract one number from another.

entries.meaning: To change a number to the nearest simpler one. ---
examples: Round your answer to two decimal places.
She rounded 4.6 up to 5.
The program is rounding every score to the nearest whole number.
entries.contrast: You round a number to the nearest ten, and round it up or down.

entries.meaning: To find the middle value of several numbers, or to reach that value typically. ---
examples: The teacher averages your four best quizzes.
He averaged a B plus for the semester.
She is averaging two hours of homework a night.
entries.русский: усреднять, выводить среднее; составлять в среднем

entries.meaning: To count things up, or for two sets of numbers to match. ---
examples: Tally the votes on the board.
She tallied the scores after the quiz.
We are tallying the results now.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (tally the votes), intransitive (the two lists tally)
entries.contrast: Consonant + -y changes: tallies, tallied, but tallying keeps the y.

entries.meaning: To work a number out again. ---
examples: Recalculate the average without the lowest score.
He recalculated his grade three times.
She is recalculating the totals after the correction.

entries.meaning: To come close to a value, or to estimate it roughly. ---
examples: You can approximate the answer before you do the arithmetic.
She approximated the cost in her head.
The model is approximating real conditions fairly well.
entries.contrast: The verb ends uh-PRAHK-suh-mayt; the adjective approximate ends -suh-muht.

entries.meaning: To put one thing in place of another, or to take someone's place for a while. ---
examples: Substitute the value of x in the equation.
She substituted for our teacher all last week.
He is substituting at the middle school this year.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (substitute the value of x), intransitive (substitute for a teacher)
entries.contrast: You substitute A for B, and you substitute for the person whose place you take.

entries.meaning: To draw a set of numbers as a line or a curve on axes. ---
examples: Today we graph linear equations.
She graphed the results on the board.
They are graphing the data by hand.

entries.meaning: To record progress or information in a table or a diagram. ---
examples: Teachers chart each student's progress every month.
We charted the class's reading speed all year.
She is charting her study hours in a notebook.

entries.meaning: To draw something as a diagram, especially the parts of a sentence. ---
examples: American students still diagram sentences in grammar class.
She diagrammed the water cycle on the board.
He is diagramming the argument step by step.
entries.contrast: The m usually doubles: diagrammed, diagramming.

entries.meaning: To arrange things in the right order. ---
examples: Second graders sequence the events of a story.
She sequenced the lessons so that the hardest came last.
We are sequencing the units differently this year.
entries.contrast: Drop the -e before -ing: sequencing.

entries.meaning: To raise a whole class's grades against a scale.
examples: Professors sometimes curve a very hard exam.
She curved the midterm by eight points.
He is curving the final grades this semester.
entries.русский: повышать оценки по кривой (о шкале оценок)
entries.contrast: In American schools, to curve a test means to adjust everyone's score, usually upward.
